sections.name: Hammer
sections.card:
Summary: A close-range item from Donkey Kong: grab it and you run across the screen swinging it back and forth nonstop. It is an extremely powerful item, but you have no recovery move while you carry it.
Uses: Grabbing it sends a player into a state that inflicts significant damage and knockback, but while swinging they cannot jump a second time in the air, use any other attacks or defend.
Tips: Every now and then the mallet head falls off and the wielder ends up completely vulnerable, swinging just the handle; from Melee on there is a 12.5% chance of this as it is picked up, and the fallen Hammer Head can be picked up and thrown as a powerful item. If an opponent is swinging a Hammer, sending them off a ledge can effectively KO them, because they cannot use special moves or a midair jump unless they somehow drop the Hammer.

sections.name: Beam Sword
sections.card:
Summary: A long-range battering item, similar in appearance to a lightsaber. It can be wielded and charged for melee attacks or thrown, like all other battering items.
Uses: As a battering item it bolsters your power and adds some options through throwing. The blade lengthens in direct proportion to the power of an attack, so it reaches its maximum size when swung as a smash attack, and the length changes depending on who wields it.
Looks like: A distinctive glowing blade that is at first about the size of a short sword.
Tips: In Melee its range significantly increases in size, particularly on charged smash attacks. Peach can pull a Beam Sword out with her Vegetable attack, but the chance is slim: 1/768 in Melee.

sections.name: Star Rod
sections.card:
Summary: A magic wand that holds 16 star shots and sends foes flying at a low angle when thrown. It works as an unusual combination of a battering item and a projectile item.
Uses: Hit opponents up close with it, or use smash attacks or tilts to shoot long-range stars that can hit from a distance. It is most powerful when Captain Falcon or Sheik performs a smash attack while holding it.
Tips: The item has only sixteen stars, and Captain Falcon's smash attack shoots off 5 stars and Sheik's 2, so they use it up quickly. When it runs out, throwing it at enemies is the more practical option: a thrown Star Rod deals powerful semi-spike knockback that can gimp recoveries or act as a general KO move. The stars are projectiles, so they can be reflected or absorbed.

sections.name: Super Scope
sections.card:
Summary: A long-range shooting item based on a Super Nintendo peripheral. In Melee, tapping the attack button fires three small shots, and holding it charges a stronger, larger shot.
Uses: Tap the attack button repeatedly for a constant stream of small shots that each do little knockback and damage; the high rate of fire gives a trapping effect, as the opponent has little or no time to act. Hold the button to charge a bigger shot. It has limited ammunition, 48 shots in Melee, and the higher charge levels use more.
Tips: In Melee you could not move while shooting it. The uncharged shots pass through opponents, so a stream can trap several enemies, but their 280 degree knockback angle makes a very weak meteor smash that is ineffective against opponents close to the stage. When it runs out of ammunition it only fires a puff of smoke, and you can throw the weapon for a little extra knockback and damage.

sections.name: Ray Gun
sections.card:
Summary: A long-range weapon that is fairly weak, but since it fires so fast it can easily juggle enemies.
Uses: It holds 16 shots. In Melee each shot deals 4% with horizontal knockback and can be fired every 30 frames, which lets it juggle opponents at low percents or carry them to the blast line at mid percents.
Looks like: Toy-like in appearance, with a fat shape, and it fires beams of green light.
Tips: The shots can be reflected or absorbed, while the gun itself, when thrown, can only be reflected. Try dropping it with a few shots left and watch your foes waste time and energy retrieving it.

sections.name: Maxim Tomato and Heart Container
sections.card:
Summary: The two healing items: each reduces the damage percentage of whoever picks it up. In Melee the Maxim Tomato heals 50% of a character's damage percentage and the Heart Container heals a total of 100%.
Uses: After you eat a Maxim Tomato and a brief moment passes, your damage meter slowly drains the amount, whether or not you pick up another item right afterwards. Damage you take while healing is subtracted from what the tomato heals: if an attack does 10% damage, you only recover 40%. Heart Containers drift toward the ground slowly and replenish 100 percentage points of health.
Looks like: The Maxim Tomato is a small red tomato with a noticeable black and white M on the front.
Tips: In the All-Star Rest Area you are given three Heart Containers that can heal all of your damage instead of the standard 100%. Due to a glitch, entering the teleporter in Melee interrupts a Heart Container's healing, so it does not fully heal you.

sections.name: Metal Box
sections.card:
Summary: A transforming item that debuted in Melee: whoever breaks it becomes a Metal fighter for a short time, much heavier but slower and quicker to fall.
Uses: In Melee the effects last 12 seconds, though the time limit decreases as the fighter takes damage, especially from fire attacks. Weight is multiplied by 3.0 and walking speed by 0.7, while falling speed and gravity are both doubled.
Tips: The faster fall makes recoveries harder. In Melee, a Metal Box hit by a projectile disappears, but disjointed attacks and any attack from a sword-wielding character still break it and still turn the attacker into a Metal fighter.

sections.name: Super Star (Starman)
sections.card:
Summary: An item from the Mario series, known as the Starman in Melee, that makes you invulnerable to all attacks for a short period of time.
Uses: All you need to do is touch it to power up. Melee repeats the first game's behaviour, where the fighter is invincible for ten seconds but does not damage opponents by touching them.
Looks like: The fighter who grabs it is given a bright, sparkling appearance.
Tips: It bounces around in large arcs and eventually tumbles out of the stage, so touch it before it falls off. In Melee its theme music lowers the stage music's volume until the stage music is extremely difficult to hear.

sections.name: Super Mushroom and Poison Mushroom
sections.card:
Summary: Two Mario items that change your size for about ten seconds. The Super Mushroom, which debuted in Melee, makes you giant, and the Poison Mushroom makes you shrink.
Uses: The Super Mushroom raises your size, strength and mass, making it harder for foes to knock you off; in Melee it multiplies weight by 1.6 and the damage of direct attacks by 1.2, but gives no armor, so you still flinch from any knockback. The Poison Mushroom takes away power and mass, making you a prime target to get smashed offscreen with even a light attack.
Looks like: The Poison Mushroom is a deceptive look-alike of the Super Mushroom, with a slightly darker coloration and angry eyes.
Tips: Both keep sliding to the right, but in Melee they slide left if they spawn on the right half of the stage. Touching one while under the effect of the other restores your normal size. In Melee, jumping at the moment a Super Mushroom's effects wear off gives a super jump almost as high as two jumps while wearing the Bunny Hood.

sections.name: Fighting Wire Frames
sections.card:
Summary: Common enemies in Melee's 1-player modes, in male and female varieties. Generally they are weak and light fighters and are very easy to KO.
Weak points: They cannot use special moves or charge smash attacks, and their moves are much weaker versions of Captain Falcon's and Zelda's attacks; they make up for having no recovery moves with high jumping. Their attacks lack any real physical strength, and they are slow and easy to outmaneuver.
Looks like: A framework of pink lines in a humanoid shape, with the Super Smash Bros. logo on the face and a red heart-like object in the chest; they are larger than the characters they are modelled on.
Tips: Males always home towards your character, while females play a more passive role and rarely attack directly. In Cruel Melee all of them are extremely aggressive, extremely powerful and harder to knock off-stage, so characters cannot survive easily among them. In Adventure Mode they are fought in a low-gravity version of Battlefield, and there and in Multi-Man Melee they cannot be Star or Screen KO'd.

sections.name: Classic Mode's final boss
sections.card:
Summary: The last fight of Classic Mode, fought on the Melee version of Final Destination. It has a set amount of HP that must be depleted to win, and in Melee that amount depends on the difficulty.
Weak points: In Melee this boss loses the ability to turn around, and its movement depends entirely on the attack it is using and your position: it always returns to its starting position when it is not attacking.
Looks like: A giant white glove; in Melee its wrist fades into nothingness instead of ending in a cuff.
Tips: Its power increases with each increment in difficulty, and the highest levels give it many attacks that can KO in one hit. Laser Nail shoots a laser beam from each fingertip; Finger Bullet fires one pair of bullets until it has taken 150% damage and three pairs after that. Power Slap buries the player, and the Vertical Throw cannot KO under normal conditions. Taking half of its HP off within the time limit brings a second boss into the fight.

sections.name: A hidden boss in Classic Mode
sections.card:
Summary: A bonus boss that appears in Classic Mode's last fight, alongside the final boss. To face it you must play on Normal difficulty or higher and reduce the final boss's HP by half within a total of 5 minutes and 50 seconds since the start of the mode.
Weak points: It starts with the same number of HP that the first boss started with, and you have only one chance to defeat it. Its Spasm attack cannot hit aerial targets, and a Finger Bomb that hits a character before it reaches the ground does only low damage with minimal knockback.
Looks like: Its basic appearance is exactly the same as the final boss's, apart from being a left hand.
Tips: Most of its attacks are stronger variations of the final boss's, plus a few of its own. Flying Punch can star KO as low as 35%, the Forward Throw can KO at low percentages without DI, and the third poke of Tri-Poke can star KO at middle to high percentages.

sections.name: Brinstar's rising acid
sections.card:
Summary: Occasionally an earthquake hits Brinstar and acid starts to rise from below, sometimes covering parts of the stage. The acid deals damage and moderate knockback, but will not KO until very high percents.
Weak points: While it is rising it generally prevents characters from being KO'd on the bottom blast line. It rises and pauses at various intervals, rarely reaching its highest point, where it covers everything except the topmost platform, and after a while it subsides.
Looks like: Yellow acid, with a large pool of it in the background under a brain-like creature.
Tips: A character who has grabbed the Super Star can avoid the acid. The fleshy parts that hold the stage together can be weakened by attacks, and while they regenerate they are fall-through. In Melee, contact with the acid makes a unique splash effect with a sizzling sound.

sections.name: F-Zero racers on Mute City
sections.card:
Summary: The thirty F-Zero Racers are a hazard on Mute City: they drive around the track continuously and damage any player on contact, sending them upwards.
Weak points: The racers can be damaged and even destroyed by explosives such as the Motion-Sensor Bomb, powerful attacks and items like the Hammer and Home-Run Bat, and immovable Pokémon like Venusaur or Charizard.
Tips: A destroyed racer's wreckage stays at the point where it exploded for the rest of the match. Touching the track while the platform is hovering over it also damages you. In Adventure Mode's F-Zero stage a giant "!" on the screen warns that cars are approaching, a hit does 35% damage, and you can jump on the pink platforms along the track to avoid them.

sections.name: Pokémon Stadium's changing terrain
sections.card:
Summary: After a varying period of time the stage transforms into a random one of four variants, each based on a Pokémon type, then reverts to the basic form and repeats the cycle. The same variant can occur twice in a row.
Weak points: The fire in the background of the Fire variant is purely aesthetic and has no gameplay effect. On the Water variant's windmill, players on the current lowest arm fall, and in Melee the arms are soft.
Looks like: The basic stage is symmetrical, with one large main platform and two floating soft platforms above it, and a large jumbotron, a crowd and fireworks in the background.
Tips: The jumbotron shows a symbol for the upcoming variation during a stage transition, so you can see it coming. Many players wait out the Fire and Rock transformations by moving to the opposite side of the stage from their opponent until the stage returns to neutral. In Melee, on the Fire variant, a character hit towards the right side of the tree's base has a chance of falling through.
